snippet.title: Always have a backup plan #homesteadlife #homesteading
snippet.description:
Power Outage Prep: Here’s How I Stay Ready ⬇️

When I bought a butchered half cow this season, the first question I got was, “What if the power goes out?” It’s a legitimate concern! The power can go out for many reasons and it would be a shame to waste this beautiful meat.

This is a reminder of how important food storage is!

For me, preparation means using multiple ways to preserve food. Relying only on a freezer isn’t realistic—if the power goes out for too long, your food could spoil, and that’s both time and money down the drain.

This actually happened to a friend over the winter and they ended up giving me all of the meat from their freezer for my dogs. So sad but went to good use!

While generators can help, they’re not my go-to. They work in short-term emergencies, but they aren’t a sustainable long-term solution for my homestead.

Instead, I focus on making my food shelf-stable. As soon as my freezer is stocked, I start canning. I preserve things like stews, chilis, soups, ribs, and ground meat. I also freeze-dry meals like spaghetti with meat sauce, lasagna, and hearty soups. These methods ensure my food is safe, even if the power fails.

My goal is simple: I want to stop relying on power or outside companies to store my food. By using a mix of preservation techniques, I create multiple backup systems.

Freeze-drying for long-term storage and canning for shelf-stable, ready-to-eat meals. Freezing is for short-term, convenient storage, never long term for me! 

The secret is variety—it’s the key to being prepared for anything. This gives me not only more security but peace of mind.

What do you think? 

#homesteadinglife #homesteadlife

snippet.title: What If America Lost Electricity for 7 Days
snippet.description:
A sudden nationwide blackout leaves America in total darkness. See how a 30-day internet outage would impact our daily survival.

By analyzing the breakdown of essential services, we look at what happens when the digital infrastructure supporting modern life ceases to function. This breakdown is intended for viewers interested in emergency preparedness and the fragility of our interconnected systems.

Understanding these risks highlights the vulnerabilities inherent in our dependence on constant connectivity. We walk through the timeline of events that would unfold during a month without access to the digital world, focusing on the reality of a nationwide blackout.

snippet.title: FEMA Has a Food List. So Does the Mormon Church. They Match
snippet.description:
FEMA responds to every disaster in America. The Mormon Church owns its own farms, grain silos, and canneries. And both of them tell their own people to stockpile the exact same foods — this video breaks down the full list.
In this video, Stockpile Man reveals the official FEMA emergency food list and the Mormon Church (LDS) long term food storage program — two completely independent organizations, one government and one religious, pointing to the same shelf stable foods. Wheat that lasts 30 years. White rice, dry beans, rolled oats, pasta, and powdered milk — all backed by BYU shelf life studies that shocked researchers.
You'll learn exactly how much food per person the LDS Church recommends storing, what FEMA says every American household should keep at home, why cooking oil is the weakest link in every stockpile, and how to package rice and beans to last 30 years using Mylar bags and oxygen absorbers for under 20 dollars.
Whether you're building your first emergency food supply or expanding a long term food storage system, this is the most documented stockpile list in America — straight from the two organizations that take preparedness more seriously than anyone else.
